opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the distinction matters more than people sometimes realize. The AI browsers you mentioned, Atlas, Comet, Dia, are essentially taking the browser you already know and putting an assistant alongside it. You're still the one at the wheel. You're looking at the page, maybe you ask the sidebar to summarize something, or you say "go fill out this form," and you watch it happen in your tab. The mental model is still "I am browsing, and I have a helper."

What we're excited about is flipping that around. The starting point shouldn't be "open a browser." It should be "here's what I want to get done." You describe the outcome, say, find me a few good options for a weekend trip that fit these constraints, or keep an eye on these listings and flag anything that matches, or handle this recurring chore every week, and the agent goes off and does the work across however many sites it needs. It runs in the background, it can run in parallel, it can run while you're asleep. You come back to results, not to forty open tabs.

So a few things differ as a consequence. One is that the interface is less about pages and more about tasks: what's in progress, what's done, where the agent needs your input. Another is that the agent needs to know when to come back to you. There are moments where a decision is genuinely yours to make, like committing money or picking between options where your taste matters, and a good experience surfaces those checkpoints rather than either barreling ahead or bothering you constantly. And third, because it's outcome-oriented, things like memory and personalization become central. If it learns how you like things done, the tenth time you delegate something should feel very different from the first.

I don't think it's either-or. There will be plenty of times you want to browse yourself, and an AI-enhanced browser is lovely for that. But for a large class of things people do on the web, they don't actually want to browse. They want the thing done. That's the gap we think agents fill.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI assistants added alongside familiar browsers with an outcome-first model where agents do web tasks across sites.

r002.rationale: It describes a task-focused interface, but does not say that the same website should appear differently depending on the user's task.

r003.rationale: It says agents can work in the background or while the user sleeps, but does not address how agents on the user's device would keep working after the laptop is closed.

r004.rationale: It presents parallel agent work as a capability, without identifying device overload as a scaling problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot. I'd say the AI browsers are really interesting, and in some sense they're the natural first step—you take the browser, which is the thing everyone already uses, and you put a model in the sidebar, or you let it read the page you're on, and maybe take a few actions. It's an incremental extension of a very familiar interface. And I think that's valuable. It lowers the barrier, it's grounded in what people already do.

But the way I think about web agents is a little different. The browser is fundamentally designed around a human looking at a page. The layout, the tabs, the back button, all of that is for a person navigating one page at a time. When you have an agent doing the work, a lot of that scaffolding is kind of irrelevant—or even gets in the way. An agent doesn't need to look at one tab at a time. It can be doing twenty things in parallel, across sites, and the question becomes less "how do I help you browse" and more "how do I get this thing done for you," where the browsing is just an implementation detail.

So I think the experience shifts from being page-centric to being task-centric. You tell it what outcome you want—book this trip within these constraints, compare these three options and tell me the tradeoffs, go deal with this customer service thing—and the agent goes and does it, and what you see is less a web page and more a kind of report of what it did, where it got stuck, what decisions it wants you to make. The surface area the human sees becomes about oversight and intent, not navigation.

The other piece that I think is really important is trust and control. With an AI browser, you're sort of watching over its shoulder, which is reassuring but doesn't scale. With a true agent, you need different primitives—being able to see what it's about to do before it does something irreversible, like making a purchase, being able to set boundaries ahead of time, having a legible trace afterward. I don't think we've figured out that interaction design yet, honestly. It's a much more open question than people think.

And then there's the question of whether the web itself adapts. Right now agents are operating on interfaces built for humans—clicking buttons, parsing visual layouts. Over time I expect we'll see more sites expose structured ways for agents to interact with them, and that changes the experience again. So I see AI browsers as a bridge, a very useful one, but I think the destination looks pretty different—something where you're interacting with the task and the agent, and the browser kind of fades into the background.

r001.rationale: It contrasts adding a model to a familiar browser interface with a task-centric agent experience where the browser fades into the background.

r002.rationale: It says the experience shifts from page-centric to task-centric, but does not propose that the same website should appear differently depending on the user's task.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss agents continuing to work after the user closes the laptop.

r004.rationale: It mentions agents doing many things in parallel, but does not identify device overload as a scaling problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is less about the browser itself and more about how much you’re delegating. With an AI browser, you’re still often driving: you’re looking at a page, asking questions, and getting help with what you’re doing. With a web agent, the starting point can be the outcome you want. You give it a task, and it figures out how to navigate across sites and carry out the steps.

That changes the experience quite a bit. Does the agent need your attention throughout, or can it work in the background? When should it ask a clarifying question? When should it come back for approval? And how does it give you enough visibility that you can trust what it’s doing without having to watch every click?

I’d expect these experiences to converge. Sometimes you want to explore and make decisions yourself, with assistance. Other times you want to delegate. The interesting design problem is making that handoff feel natural, while keeping you in control.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI browsers that assist while the user drives with web agents that start from an outcome and handle navigation and steps, conveying a shift in the interaction model.

r002.rationale: It does not propose that a website should appear differently depending on the user's task.

r003.rationale: It does not address agents continuing to work after the user closes their laptop.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss running many agents in parallel or the resulting device-capacity problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is really about how much of the experience is centered on the browser versus the task you want to accomplish. With an AI browser, you’re still browsing, and the AI can help you understand a page or take actions in that context. With a web agent, you might start by expressing an intent, and the agent figures out which sites to visit and how to get the task done.

So the experience could become less about navigating tabs and more about giving direction, reviewing options, and approving consequential actions. But those aren’t necessarily separate categories. I can imagine browsers becoming the place where you collaborate with agents—where you can see what they’re doing, step in when needed, and hand things back. A lot of the design challenge is figuring out when the agent should act independently and when it should bring you into the loop.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI helping within the browsing experience with a web agent that starts from a task and chooses sites and actions to complete it.

r002.rationale: It does not propose that a website should look different depending on the user's task.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss agents continuing to work after the user closes their laptop.

r004.rationale: It does not identify parallel workflow agents overwhelming the user's device as a scaling problem.
